subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF INQUIRY INTO CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH AIRCRAFT OPERATE IN NORTHWESTERN ONTARIO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. It is in regard to a series of crashes which have taken place in northwestern Ontario and the fact that pilots have now circulated a petition calling for an inquiry into the conditions under which private aircraft and public aircraft are operated in northwestern Ontario. I wonder if the minister could indicate to the House whether he has changed his mind as to whether an inquiry is necessary under these new circumstances?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF INQUIRY INTO CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH AIRCRAFT OPERATE IN NORTHWESTERN ONTARIO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very conscious of the concern in northern Ontario regarding air safety and the reports arising out of recent incidents. After a similar situation some time ago, I conducted an investigation and determined that the parallels, in terms of their safety and precautions, were about the same in that region as in other parts of the country and that the highest Canadian standards were indeed in place. However, the recent incidents and the concern have led me to ask for a further investigation into the situation. That is now going on. 1 am willing to say that if that investigation reveals the need for a more formal inquiry, I will be happy to see that that is undertaken as well. The present fact appears to be that the standards and rules are adequate. The question is whether there are reasons, including economic pressures, for them being contravened. Of course, we would want to come to grips with that very important question.

subsubtopic: SPRUCE BUDWORM IN NOVA SCOTIA-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct my question to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment who is also responsible for the federal forestry policy. In view of the fact that in Nova Scotia some two million acres of forest land are under some form of spruce budworm attack which will result in an eventual loss of some six million cords of spruce and balsam fir, causing a major catastrophe throughout our province, the economy of which is based on our forest industries, will the minister indicate, either today or when convenient, whether his department plans to assist contractors in harvesting the devastated areas and whether he has any ongoing plans of a long term nature to assist Nova Scotia during this difficult period?

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
subsubtopic: SPRUCE BUDWORM IN NOVA SCOTIA-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the decision to spray or not to spray in the case of the spruce budworm attack is one that rests with the provincial authorities which, under our constitution, are responsible for the management of forests. The federal government is obviously involved in research on spruce budworm. In fact, over $30 million have been spent and a further increase in that amount will be made by a co-ordinated effort between Canada and the United States into the research aspect of the problem. Management practices, such as early harvesting, can in fact solve certain problems, and that appears to have been Nova Scotia's decision. We had not become involved in this part of their activities, nor do we intend to at the moment.

subsubtopic: CATTLE-MEASURES TO SAFEGUARD TRADE WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture, and it deals with last Monday's United States announcement of new import restrictions against certain Canadian cattle as a result of a new round of non-tariff barrier trade irritants and with particular regard to the recent brucellosis issue which could involve Canadian cattle. Can the minister assure the Canadian beef and dairy industries that his recent personal discussions with Mr. Bergland will preserve and hopefully safeguard Canadian cattle trading interests in our two-way cattle trade with the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: CATTLE-MEASURES TO SAFEGUARD TRADE WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I can reassure at least those producers of purebred

cattle who have followed good health practices that the negotiations which took place between Mr. Bergland and myself were based on a realization of the importance of the two-way trade between our nations. For those people who have had their herds tested within the last 12 months and who have had any additional cattle they have added to their herds in the last three months tested, there will be no impediment in the export of their cattle.
We realize, and I am sure the hon. member realizes, that we need to tighten up our procedures for trying to eradicate brucellosis. I am sure the hon. member is aware that our rate of brucellosis is lower than the rate in the United States. The United States has some areas which are called brucellosis-free, and we have some as well. When these are published, we will be negotiating with the United States on this contract. I see some loss of export trade at the present time, but 1 do not look on that as a trade barrier. I look on it as strictly a health move, and contrary to what some people have suggested, I emphatically deny that it is a trade barrier the United States has imposed. It is a health measure.

BLUE TONGUE-POSSIBILITY OF REDUCTION IN TESTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I suggest that up until now the discussions seem to indicate that Canada is the loser. speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: BLUE TONGUE-POSSIBILITY OF REDUCTION IN TESTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we touched on that. They commend the program we have. I disagree with what some people from the Canadian Cattlemen's Association are reported in press reports to have said. They have said that it is a trade retaliation move. I emphatically deny that because Mr. Bergland has no intention of doing that. I have a harmonious relationship with the American Department of Agriculture, and the relationship I have with the present Secretary of Agriculture is the best there has been for years.

Clearly, that implication was contained in the hon. member's statement. I rise seriously on a question of privilege because I think such a remark constitutes most inappropriate behaviour on the part of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton.
Let me refer to what happened when this matter was raised in the House of Commons, back on October 27. A copy of the Spectator was flown in from Hamilton for the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). The hon. member had that copy in his possession almost contemporaneously with the appearance of the edition on the street in Hamilton on that day. He rose and quoted a story alleging some political interference on my part. 1 immediately got in touch with my solicitors and launched a libel suit against the Spectator. The matter is now before the courts.
I believe the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton is well aware of that activity on my part. He must also be aware that my making statements now about those allegations in the Spectator would not be the wisest course for me to follow. Now that the matter is in the hands of my solicitors it is up to them to pursue it in the courts to its normal conclusion. Therefore freedom of expression on my part is limited at this time.
The Spectator printed an apology, an apology which, in the opinion of my solicitors, was not sufficient, and we are continuing the law suit.
What has the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton done? Using the excuse of his unhappiness with certain written answers provided to questions yesterday, the hon. member rose in his place and tried to "muddy up" a political personality who happens to be on the side opposite to him.

subsubtopic: INCENTIVES AVAILABLE FOR DEVELOPMENT OF RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES
speechtext: Are tax incentives, grants, or other industrial research incentives available to the private sector of the economy for research and development of renewable energy sources and, if so, what are they?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: INCENTIVES AVAILABLE FOR DEVELOPMENT OF RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is concerned: The federal government has a number of initiatives to encourage the use of renewable energy sources. These include: (a) The 1976 budget measures which increased the Capital Cost Allowance for certain types of equipment which produce energy from waste and the elimination of federal sales tax on solar energy equipment and heat pumps, (b) Current and operating expenses for research and development conducted by the private sector into renewable energy sources are eligible for an investment tax credit of 5 percent, 7 Vi percent or 10 percent depending on where the activity is undertaken, (c) Under the Enterprise Development Programme grants are available to private industry to encourage research and development in commercial activities including renewable energy sources, (d) The National Research Council has a research, development and demonstration program in cooperation with the private sector respecting the use of solar energy in heating applications for buildings.
In so far as the Department of Finance is concerned: Research and development for renewable energy sources falls within the general incentives of the Income Tax Act. Thus section 37 of the Act provides that a taxpayer may deduct in the year incurred any expenditures on scientific research, including those of a capital nature, to the extent that the scientific research is related to a business carried on by the taxpayer. It should also be noted that certain types of equipment which contribute to the efficient use of certain energy resources can be written-off for tax purposes over two years. The equipment which qualifies for this favourable treatment is described in class 34 of Schedule B to the Act.

speechtext:
It has to be said that this minority report to which I refer, submitted by Mr. Gratton and Mr. Tarnopolsky, represented the views of two of the four commissioners. Members from other regions-and this is my real point-I fully understand may also be less than satisfied with the redistribution process and the decisions of their electoral boundaries commissions. But in no other case and in no other province have members of independently appointed boundaries commissions, specifically members appointed to a commission by the Speaker of this House, filed a minority report recommending redress by parliament.
That is why this case is different from any other grievance filed, and understandably filed, by members in different parts of this country. The commissioners Gratton and Tarnopolsky, referring to a disagreement within the commission with respect to the interpretation to be given to section 13 of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, and with specific reference to the problem of determining whether the region of northern Ontario should have assigned to it 12 or 11 electoral districts, said:
The function to be exercised is the proper distribution of electoral districts on a representation by population basis, qualified by the necessity or desirability of giving effect to such human consideration as "community or diversity of interest" and by practical elements such as geographic considerations including in particular the sparsity, density of population of various regions of the province, the accessibility of such regions, etc.
They went on to say this, and it is the official comment of the minority report of the commission:
There has been overwhelming evidence that the region of northern Ontario comes within these qualifying provisions. The desirability if not the necessity of allocating as many seats as possible to that region has been manifestly demonstrated.
And later, referring to the stricture imposed by parliament with reference to the 25 per cent variable above or below the provincial quota, they said:
We believe that the fundamental question is: should the commission, where special consideration seems necessary, deal with a "region" of Ontario, or should its fundamental basis of consideration be all electoral districts in relation to the electoral quota?
We feel that the former could have been done within the terms of section 13, without violating its intent.
Notwithstanding the very clear and strong suggestion contained in these words, it was clearly the position of the commission that this House of Commons has a responsibility to act in this situation.
May I refer Your Honour's attention to the words of the Representation Commissioner, Mr. Castonguay, spoken at the public hearing held in Thunder Bay on October 9, 1975, when he referred to the issue of maintaining 12 seats in northern Ontario. He said:
I maintain it should be done by legislation. Parliament should specifically instruct this commission as other legislatures have done. They should be the ones judging this, not us.
Later the Honourable Mr. Justice Grant, Chairman of the Commission, at page 55, said on the issue of 12 seats in northern Ontario:
Your remedy lies in parliament, does it not, not with us?
Finally, Professor Tarnopolsky later in the same hearing on the issue of the recognition of northern Ontario as a region, speaking to the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Penner), stated at page 89 the following:
If I may, I disagree with whoever advised you or parliament on how much you could have done. And I am sure you can find people who could write a pretty good legal brief for you that there is more parliament could have done in order to ensure a region within a province got special consideration. I don't think it was impossible. Either you were misled or could have countered better. But I think it is something parliament could have taken care of better if they had wanted to.
In increasing the number of constituencies in Ontario from
95	to 96, would Ontario representation in this House be disproportionate to that of other provinces? The average population per constituency in all other provinces is as follows: in Newfoundland with seven seats the quotient would be 74,586; in Prince Edward Island with four seats it would be 27,910; in Nova Scotia with 11 seats it would be 71,723; in New Brunswick with 10 seats it would be 63,455; in Quebec with 75 seats it would be 80,370; in Manitoba with 14 seats it would be 70,589; in Saskatchewan with 14 seats it would be 66,160; in Alberta with 21 seats it would be 77,518; and in British Columbia with 28 seats it would be 78,022. Ontario has the highest quotient with 95 seats and an average of 81,085. With
96	seats its quotient will be, based on the 1971 census, 80,240. With the exception of Quebec, which will be only marginally higher by 130 people, Ontario's quotient will still be 2,000 people greater per constituency than the next highest province, which is British Columbia. Therefore there would seem to be no validity to the argument that Ontario, by the operation of this proposed legislation, would receive a disproportionate degree of representation and be favoured over any other province.
In concluding, I should ask all members to consider this seriously. We in this party, and particularly the northern Ontario members, consider that this is not gerrymandering. This is based on a principle which has been recognized by the Electoral Boundaries Commission. The only redress available to us is by the action of this House. There has been overwhelming evidence that the region of northern Ontario comes within the qualifying provisions of the act at 12 seats. The desirability, if not the necessity, of allocating as many seats as possible to that region, has been manifestly demonstrated. I ask for the support of the House in passing this bill.

The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) gave an example of distances between towns being 1,400 miles. That is the length of the entire maritime provinces. It would probably take in Newfoundland as well. In one case it would be necessary to travel 1,400 miles to reach a community where there are 4,500 people. What will happen to those people? We are talking about an electoral district of well over 100,000 people. Nobody will bother about those people. No political candidate will go there. The Liberal government may drive in a new fire truck for them, but they will not see a candidate. Thus, they are really isolated. Money has never been provided to make that kind of representation possible in northern Ontario.
We belong to 12 districts that are totally different than southern Ontario which is organized by counties. In northern Ontario we are organized in a different way mainly because of communications. Many of these communities can only be serviced by air. Some of them can only be serviced by train, and some by boat. Many of the communities are very remote and very difficult to service.
The minister has said that the Speaker appointed the commissioners. I argue that point. They were appointed by the provincial government. One of the problems we had was that the people the provincial government supplied, the judge and one of the commissioners, represented the provincial government rather than the interests of federal representation.
Perhaps we are only paying lip service to the idea of representation, but I suggest the minister should be willing to include Quebec. Northern Quebec is included in that whole

northern area. The new parts of Quebec which the federal government turned over to that province not long ago, and a great deal of the rest of Quebec, are now in two ridings, not three. The area in one riding is bigger than the whole area of the prairie provinces.

Yes, certainly, the riding of the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) is huge. At one time a third of this country was in one riding, but the House saw fit to divide it into two ridings, not because of the population but because if someone is to be elected to represent that area, it should not only be in name but in fact, and it was impossible at that time to cross the Arctic from east to west. It is hard enough to travel in that area from north to south. We saw fit to give the area two representatives to serve the population there. They are not considered second class citizens. We tried to make them first class citizens like everyone else.
If this bill is approved, it should have attached to it a commitment from the government that we will also give northern Quebec one extra seat, because if we want to provide proper representation for the people, it should be a two-way street.
It might be said that if you cannot get to the people and they cannot get to you, then perhaps they should communicate with you by mail. But the fact of the matter is that it takes Five days for a letter from Kirkland Lake-or wherever the place may be-to get to Ottawa, so how long would it take for a letter from Port George to arrive in Ottawa? It would take weeks. Sometimes an airplane has to stay there for two or three weeks because it cannot get back. I suppose it carries mail.
There can be no representation unless you are able to communicate with the people. It seems to me that if the government wanted to get away from charges of gerrymandering being made by some, there must be a commitment that a seat will be given to northern Quebec as well.
This legislation affects my riding. In fact it affects all the ridings in northern Ontario. I am quite prepared to run there as the riding is now, and also as it will be. 1 can speak personally because now I will have a community with about

It seems to me that representation by population will not be affected by the allocation of this additional seat in northern Ontario. Mr. Speaker, the minister stated a while ago that it was essential to grant an adequate representation to northern Ontario. When the readjustment was made in northern Ontario, it was thought advisable to reduce the number of constituencies from twelve to eleven and in northwestern Quebec from three to two.
Today, on the basis of a specific issue, that is the report on which the commissioners were divided, the same argument comes up again, that northern Ontario should be given an additional constituency since the northern Ontario area covers 80 per cent of the Ontario territory. I readily accept these arguments and I think that it would be useful to have an increased representation that would not alter the Electoral Act.
But 1 feel that the minister made a mistake when he refused to recognize the fact that north western Quebec, with an area covering almost 60 per cent of the Province of Quebec has only two constituencies, as a result of redistribution. One is the Villeneuve riding, which occupies nearly half the area of the Province of Quebec, where, as the hon. member who spoke before me indicated, there are communities 1,400 or 1,500 mile away from one another. In sparsely populated areas, distance is a main factor in a constituency. But I feel we should also consider the importance of communications between individuals. When an hon. member has to fly over an area of such dimensions, because roads are few and far between, he certainly needs more time than is required to cover an urban riding in downtown Montreal.
When we made representations to the commissioners during hearings in northwestern Quebec and requested that this third major constituency be maintained, our request was turned down on the basis of statistical data of the 1971 census. I understand that their ruling had to be based on these data, but they failed to recognize the fact that some 6,000 people have' moved into this region since 1971 to work on the James Bay project, and that there will be some 15,000 workers there one year from now, which means an increase of 15,000 people. Unfortunately, the commissioners refused to consider this. They unanimously ruled that these 15,000 new residents are not important for Quebec.
It is important that Ontario should have adequate representation, but Quebec, no, we must abide strictly and legally by the figures provided by the 1971 census. To be logical and reasonable, the minister should immediately add a third electoral district in the province of Quebec, if the arguments he raised for Ontario are to be consistent. I see absolutely no difference between the two situations. It is true that these are large electoral districts. It is true that the constituents must be served. It is true that people must be provided with the best of services. There again, the minister contends that by establish-

ing an additional electoral district in northern Ontario, this would not significantly lower the average representation but would allow for a better balance and Ontario would have an average population of 80,200 people per riding while Quebec has an average of 80,300 inhabitants per riding.
A fair provincial average would be achieved by adding one electoral district in northwestern Quebec. This would probably reduce the average per riding in the province of Quebec by about a hundred votes. However, this would resolve the geographical and physical problem one has to face. The Minister said a while ago that at a given point, we must consider, when accepting or adding a new constituency, the geographical aspects as well as the access to such places.
I think that if the Minister were to ask the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) for maps of the provinces of both Quebec and Ontario, he would have an idea of the territory to be covered by only one or two members in northwestern Quebec. Finally it is unfortunate that the province of Quebec should be discriminated againjt in this matter. According to the figures, I am willing to admit that the report was incomplete and that it was not unanimous while the one concerning Quebec was unanimous. On the other hand, one thing is certain: in Ontario, or in northern Ontario, constituencies are much more flexible politically-speaking. While in northwestern Quebec, in the last 15 years, the people have voted exclusively for the Social Credit Party of Canada, and have never given any votes to the Liberal Party. And the commissioners were not appointed by the Social Crediters either. However, when we happened to discuss the matter with them, we felt that political implication.
I feel the minister would meet with approval if he included in his bill specific recognition that a new riding is required in northern Ontario, as well as the clear and specific addition of a new riding in northwestern Quebec. Thus, justice would really be done to the people of both areas. The addition of one riding in Quebec would certainly not upset the national representation profile nor the representativeness of each hon. member. But it would really solve the problem of the area to be covered and the capacity of representation of the hon. members. One does not have to wonder about the shape of the road in that part of the country. They have dirt roads and, in the case of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), he will have to go around by train, while in northwestern Quebec there is not even a train, and air service is still inoperative. It must be that in the mind of the minister the hon. member elected in that part of the country would probably have to go around for a while riding a deer or a moose to visit the people. But that is not taken into consideration.
In closing, I ask the minister to take our requests into consideration and to combine with his bill, Bill C-421 introduced by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette); then I feel the intentions or pronouncements of the minister will really mean something when he speaks of serving the people. And then only when the two bills are grouped, or at least when the minister has assured us that Bill C-421 introduced by the
July 20, 1977

hon. member for Villeneuve will also be accepted, then only will northwestern Quebec be adequately represented.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am a city dweller, and too rarely in this House do we hear the point of view of urbanites expressed.
I think there is a great consciousness among Canadians wherever they live, that concessions must be made; that we must not insist absolutely on representation by population in a country as diverse and widespread as Canada. However, what has been said here today so far raises questions about the equity of our system of parliamentary representation, and about the trend represented by this bill and the one just referred to by the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette). That trend seems to be away from recognition that Canada is increasingly an urban society. Whether we like it or not, that is the Canada of today and of the future. While all of us want to make every concession for the preservation of a feeling of identity by all Canadians with their country and with their national government, we must surely take care that in making these concessions to alleviate the disparities in Canada we do not ignore the strains which can be placed on our society by increasing disparity of political representation in our national institutions.
In introducing this bill the minister said that it is based on principle, and I hope that my remarks will be taken as being similarly based on principle. The minister made reference to the populations of various provinces and argued very cogently that Ontario is not over-represented, from the standpoint of population, under the present distribution of seats in this parliament or the proposed one. But he did not make a comparison between the populations of southern Ontario and northern Ontario, as he might have done, and 1 think it would assist hon. members if the minister were able to show that his bill would not increase the disparity of per capita representation which already exists between the more densely populated part of Ontario and the less densely populated part.
The minister made reference to the distances involved. I want to remind hon. members that, in the modern society in which we live, density can be as serious a factor as distance in alienating the population from its institutions. As those of us who live in the great cities of Canada know, there is such a thing as high-rise isolation. We know that it is often difficult for people in a densely populated part of a large city to feel close to their elected representative and to communicate with him, and it is hard for their representative, in turn, to communicate with his constituents.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) mentioned that there are distances of 1,000 or 1,400 miles between some small communities and the minister referred to the huge land mass of northern Ontario. We all recognize that is true of northern Ontario, northern Quebec, and other parts of Canada. The present law recognizes the difficulties in transportation, communication, and representation in such large
Ontario Representation
land masses. However, 1 want to remind hon. members that we represent not land, but people. We are not called upon here to speak for acres-or perhaps hectares, after the metric system is in force-we are called upon to speak for our constituents who are people, and I ask hon. members to remember the constant whittling away of the principle of representation by population which we have seen in this House in recent times.
The system of redistribution is already biased against urban areas. One only has to look at the riding which I have had the honour to represent since I was first elected in 1965. Between 1965 and 1968, when a redistribution occurred my riding had in it the largest number of people of any riding in Canda. Since 1968, after a redistribution of seats, my riding has continued to have the largest number of people in it. Even after the redistribution, which is to take place at the next general election, the three ridings which will be created mainly from my present riding will still be among the largest of Canada's federal constituencies.
Not only does the present formula militate against the people of my area receiving adequate representation by population, but the law has been interpreted by the Electoral Boundaries Commission in Ontario in such a way as to prevent it from taking into account any projection of population. Given even the fairest of formulas, even if you accept the formula now in the law, there will occur some distortion in the representation of urban dwellers in a rapidly growing area, because the projection of population between periodic redistributions is not taken into account.
1 did not rise to oppose this bill. I would not argue strenuously against the present bill or the one the hon. member for Villeneuve proposed. I think I speak for my constituents, the people of Toronto at large and urban dwellers of Canada generally, when I say we are prepared to make any concession which will keep this country united and allow people to identify strongly with Canada and its national government.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
However, we are an urban society and becoming increasingly urbanized. Not even urban dwellers are entirely in favour of this trend. Personally, I wish it were otherwise. But when we speak in this House of representation, we are surely not speaking of spaces, of cities, or of distances in this country. Surely we speak of the people we represent. We must be conscious of this country's realities.
City dwellers do not insist on perfect justice, but they ask members of the House, when considering changes to electoral law to remember that we represent people and nothing else. If we remember this and do this, we shall avoid arousing in city dwellers the sense of isolation which is evident, in a political sense, in some of those living in the far reaches of our country, and we shall preserve in all our citizens their sense of identification with Canada, which is an objective we surely all share.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are considering an extremely important matter, not only for the residents of the province of Ontario, but also for the whole country, because until 1965 the distribution of electoral districts was the responsibility of Parliament and all governments in our history have tried to ensure fair representation for rural areas, accepting the fact that these areas had a lower density of population than urban centres.
We must still endeavour to maintain harmony in our country so that in all provinces, including the province of Quebec, Canadian citizens will be satisfied to have an equitable number of people representing them in the Canadian Parliament. Because Parliament has surrendered this responsibility through legislation, the task of establishing and redistributing electoral districts has been turned over to commissions. Today the government feels it should not have done that, as the minister mentioned in his speech, and should have kept its right to have the final word after the reports of these commissions have been submitted to the minister responsible for this issue.
And today the government feels obliged to intervene through a very special bill to give one more representative to the province of Ontario, on the basis of very logical arguments. However, if these arguments are logical in the case of Ontario, they are just as logical for the province of Quebec with regards to the Canadian northwest. Hon. members have had discussions about this issue long before today.
I had the opportunity myself to take part in discussions and there seemed to be an agreement on the fact that this should be done under the same bill for Ontario and Quebec. Today, we hear only rumours. As there was no official statement, we try to read the minds of hon. members from other provinces: if we allow Quebec another hon. member, an additional electoral district, other provinces will demand the same thing. I for one would like to hear evidence on this in Parliament and not behind the scene.
In any case, we should always apply good horse sense. The minister responsible for the Electoral Boundaries Act who sponsors the bill should perhaps give further consideration to this, and add provisions to ensure that Parliament regains control, that it has the last say in the distribution of electoral districts. I suggest this, in all fairness, concerning the Electoral Boundaries Act of our country.
Mr. Speaker, we have already dealt with the matter of area and population. In Quebec, the quota is roughly 80,000. As 1 said in this House on April 6, twelfth-graders could have done the same work as our distinguished judges. They simply had to add up the population according to the census and to distribute the population and then draw up boundaries. Indeed, this is how it was done in our province even though we made representations in all sincerity and even though ten members of Parliament signed a joint letter. We were unanimous; it was not a question of partisanship, but of justice and common

sense. In my area, ten members signed a joint letter which was forwarded to the Quebec Commission but was not even acknowledged. I cannot understand this. The Commission was so engrossed in its powers that it did not even acknowledge the letter. They do their job and then, whether you like it or not, they submit their report. If you are not satisfied, that is too bad! I finally understood that this is what the commission meant.
Mr. Speaker, I heard the comments of the previous speaker a while ago and I thought that they did show real good sense; he said that people living in high-rise apartment buildings do not have as many chances of coming into contact with their representatives. They do not have as many opportunities as the people living in rural constituencies, but there is another side to the story. In rural constituencies, people in general know their representatives and arrange to meet them, and when we look at the map of any constituency, be it Abitibi, Villeneuve and Temiscamingue, which I know somehow better, or Bellechasse, which I know very well, we realize that the member of Parliament has to travel far and wide in order to meet his people. Whatever may be the number of inhabitants in a town or a municipal community, these people live there and they are entitled to the same consideration from their member as if the population were 2,000. This is how I understand my role as a member of Parliament. In the constituency of Bellechasse, there are 83,000 people. It is a rural constituency. There is only the city of Montmagny and the balance is made up of rural communities.
So under the act the commissioners had the authority to increase by up to 25 per cent the population in a rural riding, 25 per cent of the ratio set for the province, or to decrease that population by up to 25 per cent in rural ridings. So I wonder how they have considered the riding of Bellechasse, since rather than decrease its population, because it is a rural riding, they increased it. I understand that there again there is something to change in the Elections Act in order to adjust it better to the circumstances and needs of our country.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to address particularly the Liberal members of the province of Quebec who now ensure the government majority. But I am not addressing those members as Liberal members but as representatives of Quebec ridings to ask them to support the claims we are now making for the province of Quebec, in northwest Quebec, so that an additional riding be provided in the same manner as it is done now with Bill C-60.

My colleague the hon. member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Gendron) knows quite well how I worked with him and all the others, all the efforts we made to try and preserve at least the riding of Riviere-du-Loup-Temis-couata, and my colleague is indicating that what I am telling you is the truth. July 20, 1977

I would want to fight, I want to fight for a possibility, even if it means coming back a little later if the circumstances permit, but for the time being, what we are demanding, what we are asking is that the rights of the province of Quebec be protected and that this not become a matter of division in this country but a matter of union and harmony. And I consider that if in 1977 we really want to talk with assurance to the people of Quebec about harmony in Canada, we should start by ensuring that harmony through an act of Parliament which will give us authority to talk to our fellow-citizens in our own province. So I strongly urge the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), who is sponsoring Bill C-60 on the readjustment of the electoral districts in Ontario today, to show as much enthusiasm about a readjustment for the province of Quebec.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot remain silent on the occasion of the introduction of this bill since I represent one of the ridings that will disappear in the province of Quebec. And as the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) pointed out, it is a fact that all members from Levis to Gaspe, irrespective of their political affiliation, signed a letter at the time of the debate in April asking that the riding of Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata be reinstated.
Obviously, one cannot remain silent in the face of this bill since it contains an important anomaly, namely that the whole readjustment of the electoral map was based on the premise that the province of Quebec was to be the standard on which the number of members in all other provinces would be determined. I think that nobody objects to the riding of Thunder Bay being reinstated but we would want the agreement to be maintained, that the province of Quebec should be the basis on which the number of seats in others provinces should be determined.
Then, consequently, it must definitely be accepted that there should be an additional riding in the province of Quebec. I would not want at this stage to put forth all the arguments that have been raised on this subject. I would like to tell my colleague for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) that members of this House definitely do not represent mere acres of land. They represent the people living on these acres of land and when people are widely scattered around there are bound to be enormous problems. When the last redistribution occured, the province of Quebec registered an increase of one riding but the Abitibi area lost one and the lower St. Lawrence area one, while the Montreal area gained two and the Quebec City area one.
However, one cannot ignore these regional disparities. One cannot ignore the wide diversity and the tremendous needs of these sparsely populated and underprivileged areas. I think that all the members representing urban areas will agree with me that when you cut 26 ridings out of one single municipality, things are indeed a lot easier, and a member needs half a day to walk through his whole riding, something we can hardly do in a year's time. In our case, the issues we have to deal with are much more diversified, and complex, ranging from sea port
Ontario Representation
projects, to customs, forest problems, resource development and countless difficulties which are increasingly making the task of the member more difficult. Accordingly, we are not actually against the rebirth of the Thunder Bay constituency, I believe it is, but we want the redistribution to remain on the same equitable basis that had been used for the province of Quebec. And I think that if, this afternoon, all political parties can agree, we can do something about it although I do not know which particular procedure we should use.
Perhaps it would be wise to adjourn the debate so that there be some kind of an agreement, or some discussion? But I think that it would be easy to reach an agreement for a general consensus in order that Ontario may get an additional riding as well as Quebec. It might also be appropriate, since the member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) and the member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) are far removed, especially in north western Quebec, if that riding were to be restored in the lower St. Lawrence area or in the Abitibi area, to reach an agreement between ourselves, in order to find a quick solution to this problem.
So, Mr. Speaker, I am taking the liberty of making this suggestion to the minister and to the leaders of the different parties in this House to the effect that we try and reach a concensus in order to solve this problem.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to express my support for this bill to restore 12 seats to northern Ontario. It should be pointed out that a minority report of the Electoral Boundaries Commission argued that because of the size of these northern constituencies and the difficulty encountered by members of parliament in serving constituents in these vast areas, larger constituencies should not be created in northern Ontario but that the number of seats remain as it was prior to the most recent redistribution, that is, 12.
I know it is the unanimous feeling of people in northern Ontario that the regions should not lose seats. Incidentally, the distribution proposal affects the people in my constituency of Sault Ste. Marie by drawing a line arbitrarily across the northern part of the city and putting part of the riding into the riding of Algoma. This proposition met with great objection from the electors of Sault Ste. Marie who argued, quite properly, that they had nothing in common with Algoma and wished to keep the riding of Sault Ste. Marie intact.
I have listened intently to the representations made by hon. members in the Creditiste party. I believe they have a valid point. They, like us, have vast areas to cover, and the current distribution has prejudiced their ability to serve their constituents adequately.
I sometimes hear from people who are somewhat suspicious about what the government is doing. They wonder whether the Liberal government would have gone to the trouble of restoring this one seat to northern Ontario if that seat had not been held by a Liberal. The fact that a similar measure was not made available to the people of northern Quebec will, no

July 20, 1977
Ontario Representation
doubt, strengthen the suspicions to which 1 have referred. However, the bill before us now concerns only the situation in northern Ontario. I fully support it and I hope it is passed, recognizing at the same time the legitimate grievances of the Creditiste members from northern Quebec. I hope the government will give us some kind of commitment that their representation will be restored. They, too, have lost a seat in northern Quebec. I know our party would be in favour of such a commitment, though I have yet to hear from the Conservative party what their reaction would be to a commitment to restore the number of seats in our neighbouring province. subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first 1 do not want to blame the President of the Treasury Board for having introduced today Bill C-60 in order that the House of Commons may give Ontario a better representation for its northern population, because they stand to lose an electoral district just as we did in northwestern Quebec. As the minister said, I know that he wants the population of northern Ontario to be fairly represented by a man who will give good service to the people in that area. Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to note today that the New Democratic Party supports our position as well as some Liberal members.
I also hope, as was already mentioned, that the minister will manage somehow to include Bill C-421 that I sponsor and thus grant northwestern Quebec the same privilege he is asking for people from northern Ontario, namely that the people from northwestern Quebec may be represented adequately in this House. Mr. Speaker, I would like to give the reasons which prompt us to ask the minister to include in his legislation Bill C-421. It is for the simple reason that at present I have a very large area to cover. Someone quoted earlier the words spoken by the Prime Minister at the time of the death of our leader, Mr. Andre Fortin, when he came to extend his sympathy to Mr. Fortin's family.
Last week I had to go not even to the limit of my riding, I could say three quarters of the way to the limit. When 1 left from here, from Ottawa, I had 250 miles to drive before reaching my riding and from my home I still had 275 miles to go to meet people who needed my services and, during the same weekend, I had to come back home and go to the other end of my riding which is 100 miles farther. The new readjustment of electoral boundaries, if I am lucky enough to be reelected at the next election as member for Villeneuve, puts me in a situation where only in car mileage from my home to the farthest limit of my riding there are 1,400 miles. 1 explained that to many hon. members on both sides of the House and they understood the claims I was making.
As I was saying a moment ago, maybe the Prime Minister thought about it, and it is perhaps the best reason for asking
[Mr. Symes.J
the House to adopt this bill with maybe an amendment which would also provide for another riding in northwest Quebec.
When we met the Prime Minister in the funeral home, he told us that ridings of that size were ridiculous. They too have large ridings in their party and they also have to travel through them. When we leave here we are not exhausted but very tired and we still have to drive hundreds of miles to go back to our ridings and then there are yet enormous distances to cover.
When 1 will be in my new riding-which will be called Abitibi-I will want to give my constituents what they expect from their representative, and I must consider going from my home to a locality which is not the most remote but where there are 4,500 people. I believe those 4,500 people have the right to be fairly represented, they are entitled to receiving the service they can expect from their member, from Val-d'Or to Fort George, the municipality which presently has the largest population and which is over 700 miles away from my home. As my colleague from Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) and the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) said earlier, how can one man adequately serve the people in such circumstances without exhausting himself?
Of course, we have also had a commission referred to earlier by the minister. A great number of people and organizations appeared before that commission to show the judge how ridiculous it was to bring the number of northwestern Quebec constituencies down to two. As an illustration, the CERDAT made tremendous representations, but the commission ignored them. Boards of trade, municipalities, mayors, town councils all appeared. I myself and the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) repeatedly urged the commissioners to try and give the people in north western Quebec an opportunity as allowed by statute to have their own elected representatives while meeting the criteria. Admittedly the commission relied on the 1971 census. At that time, with the redistribution of electoral boundaries, the 1971 census gave Temiscamingue an 83,667 population, and Abitibi an 88,164 population.
And here, I would like to ask hon. members to listen carefully to the remarks I want to make. The riding of Abitibi will have 88,164 constituents under the new electoral redistribution. There was a mistake because during the 1971 census, as the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) said so eloquently, James Bay did not exist. And before taking part in the debate on the bill before us, I got some information from Statistics Canada-and everybody could get it-about the number of people there were in the ridings of Temiscamingue and of Abitibi according to the last census which was recorded in June last. One must also include the riding of Villeneuve.
According to Statistics Canada, Mr. Speaker, in the last 1976 census there was a population of 57,739 in Abitibi, 52,810 in Temiscamingue and 61,897 in Villeneuve. James Bay had 4,500 residents, and according to Statistics Canada, there can be a rate of error, considering the time in which the survey took place-that is during the holidays-the number of people who did not answer, of about 1 Vi per cent to 2 per cent. Therefore, I have taken this 2 per cent error rate into account
July 20, 1977

which means that some 3,500 people would not have been declared during this census, and therefore we would have about 182,526 people to represent in northwestern Quebec.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we had a population of 171,831 in 1971. If you divide this number by three, you get exactly 57,265 people to be represented by three members. If you add those who were not included in the 1971 census and who are still there today, it amounts to between 7,000 and 10,000 people more. And if you refer to the end of this Parliament's mandate we will have a population of 15,000 for James Bay alone. I believe those people, even though they were not accounted for in the 1971 census, are also entitled to be represented by a member of parliament who is efficient in the House of Commons. Of course, the new electoral redistribution does not satisfy them, but I know with some goodwill-and at least several members have demonstrated theirs this afternoon-the government will adopt Bill C-421 to give a new riding to northwestern Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I could also be mean to the government, but this is not my intention. We could have mentioned ridings like Matane, which has 63,000 people, Mercier which covers about one square mile and has 67,000 people, Lac-Saint-Jean, represented by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), with a population of 67,200, Gaspe, with 60,481 people, and ourselves, according to the 1971 statistics, as I said earlier, we have 57,265 people for three members of parliament, or three ridings in northwestern Quebec. Now, Mr. Speaker, what more do we need? If we want to give some representation to James Bay, as I said earlier, we even have enough people to have three ridings.
But if we compare with 1971, there are about 2,500 to 3,000 fewer people in each constituency. Earlier, I heard the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) say how long a letter can take to go from the far end of the future Abitibi riding to Ottawa to make representations to the government for a new constituency. For my part, last winter, I went to James Bay and, unfortunately, I had to remain two days more than I had planned because of a storm, since the planes could not take off. As the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) said, I would like to give more to other areas because some have very large populations and I would like us to pass a measure in order to help these people who represent large populations and must travel great distances from one end of large ridings to another.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague who now represents the Abitibi riding also has one of the largest constituencies in the country. It may not be the largest, but it is one of the largest in the country. His riding nearly reaches up to the North Pole. This member has done fantastic work to represent his constituents, but if this same man also had to represent in addition to his own riding part of mine, that is Val d'Or, Lebel-sur Quevillon, Senneterre and Chibougamau, he would have to travel even more than at the present time since his home is even further than mine. In conclusion, I want to say that I have great
Ontario Representation
confidence in the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), who wants to give fair representation to northern Ontario. He will certainly do everything he can, as said the hon. member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Gen-dron), to try to negotiate with all the other House leaders, so that he and his constituents can be well represented and also that north western Quebec can be fairly represented in the House of Commons.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few comments to what has already been said concerning the representation suggested in this bill. I believe that the whole problem now caused by these redistributions came about when Parliament decided that it would no longer be responsible for the redistribution of electoral boundaries and handed over the work it had always done to a commission. Since then, and especially in the last ten years, we have suffered somewhat from the sickness of bureaucracy.
I do not know whether this is because we are lazy and do not want to take on extra work or because we do not wish to accept responsibility for our many mistakes, and this legislation is a mistake. But if we keep going this way, we will soon realize that we are referring to committees important parts of our work which, as members of Parliament, we should feel responsible for. As I said on other occasions, we are creating a politically irresponsible government, because those who do our work are not responsible to the people, they have not been elected by them to do that work. This does not mean by any stretch of imagination that those people are not competent. All I say is that we are entrusting them with powers and an authority that we should be exercising right here in this Parliament.
When the government set up that commission, they should have at least retained some control, and this is the objection I have to that commission. At least the government should have allowed members of parliament to make representations to the commissioners. I myself had problems with them, but I was told there was no way, I was 10 days late. Can you imagine that, when a member of parliament comes to discuss serious problems in his area, when subdivisions are made contrary to the constituency interests. It is an easy matter for a technician to sit down at his desk, pick up a map, draw a line here, another there, and so on, and the hell with the rest! But there is something more to it. The economic structure, the economic nerve center in each riding must be considered. With the last subdivision hon. members will have to cover constituencies whose nerve center is in another riding. This is beyond the imagination. Who could have thought this would ever happen?
A constituency with all unemployment insurance offices and other agencies, in someone else's area, this is what I have been given without regard for my constituents needs. An area which I used to cover, was thrown into another riding, but the people still go on dealing in my own constituency. So I have to serve them just the same, because I will not force them to drive 50 or 75 miles to the constituency where they were put by the commissioners. This is not their fault, so I serve more than 10 or 12 communities outside my own area. What else can we do

if we want to remain human in an unhuman set up? This is what I have always been blaming the commission for, like all other commissions. They do not see beyond the Act. If we go back to the old system, should the constituents have someone to blame, they will know who is to blame. They say: Who is responsible? 14,000	miles with 89,000 constituents, you will see. Try to serve a population such as this. This is nonsense. It was one in Ontario, they proved it to us but it is even more nonsensical in Quebec.

Do you think that people know this, that they are aware of this. Mr. Speaker, as 1 am quite concerned by the discussion now going on about Bill C-60, although this bill does not meet the purpose of this discussion in the true sense of the word, I want to speak for a moment or two to give my opinion on Bill C-60.
I listened to the speeches of most members, and I heard the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) say that members do not represent regions or territories, but people. Mr. Speaker, I agree on that. But if we consider how the population moved in a number of years in Canada, we realize that in a few years, the rural area will be underrepresented in the Canadian Parliament.
I read recently a report saying that in the year 2000, Canada will have a population of about 30 million inhabitants, of which 20 million will live in about 15 cities. That means that 10 million people, that is only one third, will live in rural or semi-rural areas. But, the way things are shaping, it is quite obvious that people living in rural areas are going to be under-represented in the House of Commons. I think Parliament should take steps to protect these rural people who are taxpayers and deserve to be represented at the same level as anybody else in Canada.
When we look at the difference between people living in areas such as Montreal, Quebec City, Toronto or Vancouver, and people living in rural areas, there is no possible comparison. In urban areas, they all enjoy administrative services. They only have to go around the corner and they come face to face with federal as well as provincial and municipal administrative agencies, whereas in rural districts, people have to travel miles and miles to be provided with the same services. Let us consider, for instance, the situation which prevails in Matagami, a mining town in the northern section of my constituency. When people have to go to the UIC office, they must go to Val-d'or. And that is over 200 miles away. So those people are disadvantaged compared to urban residents when they want to go and discuss their problems with executive officers of the federal government.
As for Canada manpower centres, it is again about the same thing, 115 miles from Matagami to Amos to go to a manpower office. No comparison is possible with urban residents. The riding 1 now represent, Abitibi, is the second largest riding in Canada. The largest is the riding of the Northwest Territories, and the second largest is Abitibi, which is larger than the
Ontario Representation
Yukon, larger than the four Maritime provinces combined, larger than France as well as many other European countries besides France: that is how large is Abitibi. Between Noranda North and Sugluk, there is a distance of 985 miles. Of course, we cannot get there by car, there is no road suitable for motor vehicles to go up there. We have to go by plane: you know when you go there but you never know when you come back.
My colleague for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) said before that he once was stranded there for two days before he could come back, and this has been my personal experience at Grande Baleine, when I had to wait until the temperature got somewhat better so I could come back. However, Mr. Speaker, distances are a factor in rural ridings; I mentioned mine but there are many others which, while not quite so large and so spread out are still nevertheless huge ridings. This should be taken into account and the residents of those rural ridings have the same right as urban dwellers. I insist that such circumstances must be taken into account. And when the commissioner travelled through these regions to get the opinion of these people, when the study for electoral redistribution was carried out, I wonder if these trips were made seriously or if they were only a face saving device, because proposals made by such organizations as CERDAT in northwestern Quebec and by the Union of County Councils, had been highly spoken of, but in any event their recommendations have not been taken into account, it all sounded beautiful but nothing positive came out of it.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we were all led to wonder what they were trying to get at with this. What CERDAT was indeed asking for was representation for three ridings in northwestern Quebec. The present situation, Mr. Speaker, is that Bill C-60 recommends that we maintain those 12 ridings which already existed in northwestern Ontario. My colleague for Villeneuve (M. Caouette) tabled a bill to maintain the three ridings in northwestern Quebec, and I think that to be fair minded, the minister who introduced Bill C-60 should agree to grant the same privilege to northern Quebec so that it gets the same representation it had before the last redistribution.
Mr. Speaker, if one cannot but agree that the present representation was calculated according to the average population shown from the 1971 census, it is a fact that within the Abitibi riding things have changed since. There has been the James Bay hydroelectric development and there must be at least an extra 6,000 persons who now live in that area, either as residents or as workers. And by 1981 they will realize that the construction will end within the decade. Then chances are we will come back in 1991 and scratch that riding from northwestern Quebec because the population will have decreased and we will play this way with representation of an area. Mr. Speaker, other members made representations, not only Social Credit members in this House, but members from other parties, urging the minister to reconsider his bill and

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the new electoral map was tabled in this House, several of my colleagues and I took part in this important debate and we blamed the commission for many things. Today, the bill under study, Bill C-60, gives evidence that we were right at least for Ontario, because the government itself recognizes that the work of the commission maybe did not take into account all valid considerations concerning northern Ontario. Now, the government would want to have a bill adopted to correct a bad distribution.
We, Social Crediters, agree in this respect with the government as far as northern Ontario is concerned, because the government recognizes today that perhaps the readjustments made by the commission were wrong mainly and especially-I believe it is the main argument made by the government- because of a bad redistribution, taking into account the geography of northern Ontario. I personally know this area fairly well and I can imagine and I admit it is extremely difficult to have an equitable representation in northern Ontario, a representation that would be as flexible as in some other ridings in other areas of the country.
That is why the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) wants us to pass this bill. On the other hand, the same situation occurs in the province of Quebec, and this is the point we want to make during this debate. If the government forces this bill down our throats to make us accept a bad situation in Ontario, it will be very ill advised, I think, if it does not take into consideration a similar situation due to geographical reasons in northern Quebec, or more specially in the area better known as Abitibi.
The President of the Treasury Board said at the outset that he was making this statement in the House today not for purposes of expediency but rather for the sake of principle. I agree that at the time of redistribution of electoral ridings in Canada we were motivated by principles rather than by political expediency. But the very principles that are worthwhile in Ontario are also valid in Quebec, particularly at a time when we, Social Crediters, think that national harmony, or as the government would rather call it, national unity, is in great danger.
I think this bill would seem to grant Ontario privileges which are not considered for Quebec when normally it should not be a privilege for either Quebec or Ontario. It would be correcting a situation because the Commission, as the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) suggested, acted very badly in many cases. It is disconcerting to see that-and the readjustment of federal districts is not the only instance-the bureaucracy always has the last word and today we are losing part of the day intended for the business of the House in an effort to rectify a situation pertaining to a riding or a province that was improperly treated, or if you want, whose electoral boundaries were badly distributed.

It is always the same thing, Mr. Speaker; bills come to this House, decisions come to this House, which have not-or almost never, we are not here to shoot the breeze-been discussed and approved by the members of this House. Unfortunately, in financial matters and then in all other fields, bureaucrats take the initiative, write the bills, make the decisions, introduce the bills in this House and the majority vote for what the bureaucrats decide. We all know it by experience, we pass a piece of legislation in good faith and with good intentions but later on when we look at it and we look at the regulations that public servants enacted, thought out, came up with and which were accepted by the Cabinet and the minister concerned, we no longer recognize the original legislation. Unfortunately, we are trying to make believe that our Canadian government is still a democratic government when, admittedly, our democracy has nearly become a monumental farce. The only redeeming thing is that the people are not aware of it.
The population still believes that its elected representatives make nearly all the decisions, when they actually decide next to nothing either in the economic field or in the field of finance. We are now faced with a small problem, that of delineating the boundaries of our own ridings. This work is left to the bureaucracy. A city five miles from the largest city in my riding, with a population of 45,000 people, has been added to the neighbouring constituency. On the other hand, a city 75 miles away has been added to mine. This is completely nonsensical. They want to get rid of the lakes to go to another place when the village that used to belong to my constituency is serviced by the eastern townships highway which goes through my constituency, and we now have to make a long detour or to go by canoe if we want to take more time and take a more direct route.
Mr. Speaker, these are the completely ridiculous aspects of bureaucracy, as was said earlier by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) and the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette). Once again, we have relinquished our authority. Not only have we relinquished our authority as members of parliament, but the federal government has also taken over the authority of provinces in another field. It does not concern the bill now before the House, Bill C-60, but in all areas, we have mixed up apples with oranges, we have mixed up the provincial, municipal and federal levels, and now we are ready to interfere with provincial rights in the field of education.
Mr. Speaker, with such confusion in the federal administration and the redistribution of constituencies, there are people who in the past two elections have believed themselves to be in one riding while they were in another. They wonder for whom to vote. Why? Because advertising is badly coordinated in this area. Some people come to the Longueuil office about unemployment insurance problems when they should go to the Sherbrooke office.
There are people in Saint-Cesaire who go to the Montreal office for their tax returns, instead of going to Sherbrooke. And in my riding it is no worse than in others, the situation is
July 20, 1977

quite the same everywhere. In those parishes located on the boundary of ridings, like in Saint-Hyacinthe for instance, people keep coming to see me because they got used to going to Shefford to get services provided by the federal government.
Well, this riding was removed, it was included in the county of Chambly during an election, it was moved to Shefford during another election, it was taken from Shefford in the course of another electoral redistribution and was returned to the riding of Saint-Hyacinthe. They are making fun of the people, because they think in terms of percentage. There is no problem in Canada, there is no unemployment problem, they think in terms of percentage.
They only rely on the figures of the manpower centres as regards percentages, when everyone knows perfectly well that all unemployed are not necessarily registered in the manpower centre and that they are not included either in the percentages of the unemployed, as the federal government tries to have us believe every time new statistics are released.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that in the particular context of Quebec, of Ontario and of Canada as a whole, the present argument is as follows: One wonders what will become of our country. We should not take too many steps at the present time to back up separatists, following an electoral redistribution which may be wrong, I admit, which may involve big mistakes, that is true, because there is a mistake in some area and they want to correct it in Ontario and are not prepared to do the same for Quebec. If they are not prepared to do the same in the province of Quebec, they can bloody well leave us in peace with national unity. This will be a sham! Why? Because the exact opposite will have been done of the words that were spoken. Unfortunately, that happens too often in this House. We are told one thing while the opposite is done. But to readjust ridings after an electoral redistribution has barely been completed-it became official just a few months ago-is to take advantage of a disorganized situation, I would say under the circumstances, to favour Ontario. Why? Because both the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec are poorly redistributed.
If readjustments are made in Ontario and not in Quebec, Ontario is enjoying a privilege, and national harmony then becomes but an empty word. If the same cannot be done for Quebec, then let us forget the whole thing and have elections according to the electoral map decided upon by the commissioners. As for us, Social Crediters, I inform the minister responsible for this bill that we are willing to pass it so that it can be referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections, provided the minister gives prime consideration to national harmony over electoral redistribution, especially as we are on the eve of a federal election the theme of which will be national unity.
It seems to me to be quite normal for the minister to accept that, not as a concession but as a logical fact since Quebec, in the process of the new electoral redistribution, lost one riding; it goes without saying that northern Ontario also loses one
Ontario Representation
because northwestern Quebec has lost one. Under those circumstances, the minister should accept Bill C-421 and readjust the respresentation for Quebec while doing justice to Ontario as he should, as he explained very well in this House; while doing at the same time what we preach, that is advocating national harmony for the Crediters and national unity for the Liberals.
So, Mr. Speaker, we agree on this bill being referred to the committee provided the minister assures us that Bill C-421 will also be taken into consideration by the committee with a view to making a correction and readjustment in Quebec as well as in Ontario.
1 think that with these arguments we could perhaps for once say that bureaucrats have been corrected, the bureaucrats did not tell us to do everything and that if they make mistakes we are here to correct them.
Mr. Speaker, since I know northern Ontario very well, I would like to see an additional district in Ontario because of the geographical situation. Considering also that I know very well the situation in northwestern Quebec, I would like the minister and particularly the government to consider the situation of northwestern Quebec on the same footing, not in a privileged way, not out of opportunism, but as a matter of principle for both Quebec and Ontario. I would like the minister to give us this guarantee so that we can be sure that both bills will be duly considered by the Committee on Privileges and Elections so that when the bill comes back to the House we could consider both ridings or both areas and give justice to Ontario and Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I will speak briefly, but I wish to take this opportunity to endorse some principles, from whatever side of the House they may originate. I would like to say that when it is said that service to the people goes beyond statistics, I endorse that principle and I will gladly work to that end every time I can possibly do so. I would like also, when reference is made to the readjustment of electoral boundaries, that the work of a member of Parliament be clearly understood. I think that the death of the leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada a few weeks ago is a case in point. We should not merely take this opportunity to mention it, but 1 hope that actually it will be a lesson for all hon. members and that they will act accordingly. I also wish now to speak for the members from rural areas.
I should like the Commission to know that campaigning is not an impossible art, but that it should take place under normal conditions, and this applies also and especially to rural ridings. The Commission should also take special circumstances into consideration, because it tried to establish a statistical rule to the effect that rural ridings are not high density areas. A fact remains: the costs involved in election campaigns in rural ridings are causing us extreme difficulties. I should like also to support those who say that civil servants or the bureaucracy should not depolarize our ridings. Such a bureaucratic procedure I feel should be corrected, because ridings are social entities which should be respected.

July 20, 1977

I would also like to sound the alarm against statistics and the bureaucracy. Some people predict the disappearance of the rural ridings. As far as I am concerned, I think that the future lies in the rural ridings and that one day they will put statistics to rest. I think that this is another matter of government responsibility to leave people where they are in conditions that they accept and which are acceptable. I agree with the adjustments proposed by the minister and I think that if such adjustments apply outside Ontario, they should hold in the province of Quebec or in any other province.
On the other hand, I would like to warn hon. members opposite. I would like them to know that when they give the impression that we, on the government side, are inveterate public persecutors, that we are always against the little man, I have to disagree because, in my opinion, I can easily be a Liberal member while respecting all the basic liberties and even low density areas.
I would like to add that it is not enough to say that we must not play politics but we must act accordingly. I listened earlier to the charges made by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) about this or that riding, the riding of this or that minister or member who may have a different image, and I think that is playing politics, and as long as I am in this House, I say to hon. members that I will oppose vigorously that kind of allegation.
For once, I fully agree with the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) who says that some things can and must be held against the Commission. I think this is true and this debate is a glaring proof of it. Therefore, let us recondition our bureaucracy, and I say it again, I am ready to work at it. However, and I repeat it, I am against those who say that we on the government side are always persecuting small underprivileged areas. If genuine and positive solutions are provided for the actual problems, I personally, will be ready to give my support. I will vote for the motion moved by the hon. minister. And I will even say to the hon. member for Villeneuve and his immediate neighbours that I am ready for it, and that if the vote were taken here and now, I would willingly support their proposal, because it is a common sense proposal, and I for one, as a member even on the government side, I am ready to vote for common sense.
