Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of astonishment, amazement, and regret

that I participate in this debate this afternoon. It is utterly incredible for an institution that purports to be managing a country as civilized and developed as Canada not to have settled for the next ten years or so, in a decision made in the last session of this parliament, the number of seats of which the next parliament is to be composed.
There was a great deal of debate on the issue at that time. We moved to a different method and a new approach to looking at the whole business of dividing up the pie that is Canada according to its provinces and territories. After all that debate, rhetoric, battling in committee, and the efforts of members opposite from British Columbia in particular to obtain justice for that province with regard to this distribution, we now have this bill before this parliament at this time. I find it absolutely incredible.
I find it incredible that the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) could go on television and berate the opposition for causing delay in getting government legislation through and then find, in the last days of this parliament, time being devoted to such a bill as this. It only shows the extent to which the government cares for the reputation of the Solicitor General as one who makes any sense at all when he talks to the Canadian people.
Last session we decided, after all the effort I have outlined, that the size of parliament should be increased from 264 to 282. It should be remembered that under the old rules British Columbia was going to get 26 members out of 264. When I came back here I was astonished to find that a formula had been presented which would increase the size of parliament to 280 and that British Columbia, which has grown faster than any other province in this country, was going to have just 26 members in the larger House. It was at that point I joined battle in an effort to do something about redistribution, aided by my hon. friend from Calgary Centre who also came from a rapidly growing province and was concerned about what was happening under the formula. After discussion, we set out finally a schedule which gave Ontario 95 seats and Quebec 75 seats. I have every sympathy with the argument which has been made by the-

-members from La Belle Province de Quebec today because I know that the redistribution formula for the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec is exactly the same as for the great provinces of Canada. If you want to change the situation in Ontario, you must absolutely change it in Quebec.

Nova Scotia, 11; New Brunswick, 10; Manitoba, 14; British Columbia, 28; Northwest Territories, 2. I do not think anybody in the House denies the need for an extra seat for the Northwest Territories bearing in mind the inhuman task which is given to the member who represents that region. Yukon Territory, 1; Prince Edward Island, 4. We know we can never have a one man one vote situation in Canada as long as we abide by the rules which establish a base below which provinces cannot fall in terms of representation. I am not quarrel-

ling with that situation. Saskatchewan, 14; Alberta, 21; Newfoundland, 7, making a grand total of 282.

I can understand the despair of Ontario members from any party which represents the north of the province. Members opposite cannot argue against that description, otherwise they would not have brought in this bill. The bill before us is a most damning criticism of the commission and of the redistribution. I have every sympathy with members of the New Democratic Party who favoured nonpolitical commissions. Whatever some members thought about it, the decision was made by this parliament long ago. The first commission in British Columbia gave us Okanagan-Kootenay-I have not had too much regard personally for them ever since. But if we are going to change the principle and go back to the old business of gerrymandering, if we are going to revert to the practice of people in back rooms dividing up a province, let us at least be honest about it and bring in a bill which does that. But do not damn the commission, and do not damn the system by bringing a bill such as this before parliament.
I will read a few more statistics, in Sudbury the person who came second received 13,200 votes. In Parry Sound-Muskoka the person who came second polled 11,000 votes. In Nickel Belt the person who came second polled 13,000 votes, and in
Ontario Representation
Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton the person who came second polled
13,000	votes. So there is a situation in which you can come in second in Northern Ontario and still have thousands more votes than it takes to win in downtown Toronto. That is where the scandal lies and that is the problem the commission should have rectified. But it did not.
One can only assume that the members of the commission are the type of people who, once they have climbed to the top of the CN Tower and looked around, think they have not only seen all of Canada, but all of Ontario too. That is our problem today, but it should not be. I did not hear any member from northern Ontario picketting the commission for what it did. Borrowing a tactic from British Columbia, did anyone strip in front of the commission, or, taking a tactic from Viet Nam, did anyone immolate himself in front of the commission? Drastic action was required at the time. Someone should have been prepared to say, "This is wrong."

speechtext: It was taken to court twice.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext:
An hon. member has mentioned that it was taken to court. And, of course, the case was lost in court. Again we are on a most dangerous course where the Parliament of Canada undoes the work of the courts of the land.
We in this country are in a situation where people are raising serious questions about whether the checks and balances that we have are sufficient. Certainly one thing we do not want to do is to turn this institution of parliament, which is the final court, into one which spends its time eliminating the work and effort of the lower courts. There is no excuse for the bill. I cannot accept that the solution lies with members from Quebec who suggested that if Ontario gets one more member they should have one more.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext: That is not the argument.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext:
There is logic there. But it should be remembered that the Parliament of Canada sits on the boundaries of those two provinces and that none of the 170 representatives from those two provinces have the problems of distance which we British Columbians have, we who are still under represented here.
I speak today as a representative from my province which did not obtain justice in that previous bill. We held our own- 26 out of 264, 28 out of 282. A formula was put forward which would add one more seat to British Columbia, but even that was not just. The formula had three categories, or four really: the ones that are set by statute, the small provinces, the intermediates, and the large.
I suggested that the solution to the problem was to treat Alberta and British Columbia as intermediate provinces, a category which they fitted. When I did my arithmetic it worked out to 29 seats for British Columbia, using the arithmetical average. It was at that point that the representative on that side told me one evening that the government would be prepared to accept 28. We had held our own, and at that point

Ontario Representation
there was not much use fighting any longer because I could see that we were not going to get the 29 seats.
This is not a private member's bill; the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) is responsible for this mess, and if I had known that the government was going to bring in a bill to upset what had been decided on and passed by parliament, then I can tell the House that I would have fought much harder and longer to sustain the demand for 29, which would have been a little closer to justice for British Columbia.
Let hon. members not forget-and this may be an argument for the NDP-that we have only six seats in the Senate. So my province is under-represented in this institution in every way.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext: Do not expect us to cry over that.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext: I am amazed-and here I come to the most crucial point of all-how the President of the Treasury Board can bring this bill into parliament at a time when the government pretends to be exercised over national unity.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext:
That is the mark of shame, of disgrace, of folly and downright silliness so far as this bill is concerned. We set up extra parliamentary commissions, celebrate Dominion Day by another name at the cost of millions of dollars, and are doing any number of things for the sake of national unity. Yet the government brings in a bill which strikes at the core of national unity and endeavours to separate in representation in this Chamber the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec As a British Columbian who believes passionately in a country from sea to sea, I find that utterly unacceptable. The government is engaging in this paltry exercise when only a few
days of this session are left, and pretends it wants to get the immigration bill through the House, along with several others.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext: And we will.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext: They are cowards and traitors.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION AND ELECTORAL DISTRICTS READJUSTMENT ACT (ONTARIO) MEASURE RESPECTING READJUSTMENT OF ONTARIO ELECTORAL DISTRICTS
speechtext:
I cannot understand why we have not heard from the members of la belle province over there.

Where is the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) and where is the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Duclos)? How can hon. members from Quebec vote for that bill? They cannot.

They can't go home and say that they let the cause of national unity down. Because this bill will be a symbol of what this government, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and the President of the Treasury Board care about national unity. Better to have brought in a bill on the national anthem, which I would have supported. I was on that committee in the Twenty-Seventh Parliament which reported unanimously, but the bill has never been presented to the House. It will not be necessary for the government to bring in a bill on the national anthem because this bill will be the symbol, will be the sign, will be the word indicating how much this government really cares about national unity.

speechtext: Hear, hear.
